title: How Election Year Market Impact Shapes U.S. Stock Returns
summary: Election years bring market volatility, but history shows fundamentals like corporate earnings and Fed policy matter more than political outcomes. The S&P 500 has gained in roughly 95% of 12-month periods following midterm elections since 1938.
body_markdown:
Election years — both presidential and midterm — tend to generate elevated anxiety among investors. The **election year market impact** is real, but research suggests it is frequently overstated. Historical data shows that **stock market volatility during midterm election years** has been higher than average, yet markets have often rebounded strongly in the year that follows. Understanding the historical patterns can help investors make more disciplined, long-term decisions.


---


## Key Takeaways


-


Presidential election cycle theory suggests midterm years produce the weakest average returns, while pre-election years are historically the strongest.


-


The S&P 500 has posted price gains in the 12 months following midterm elections approximately 95% of the time since 1938.


-


Policy uncertainty — not the winning party — has historically driven election-year volatility.


-


Corporate earnings, Federal Reserve policy, and broader economic conditions have been more consistent drivers of long-term returns than election outcomes.


-


Long-term investors may benefit from staying disciplined and avoiding portfolio changes driven solely by political speculation.


*Past performance does not guarantee future results.*

## Part 1. Presidential Election Cycle Theory and Average Stock Market Returns


### 1.1 What Is the Presidential Election Cycle Theory?


The **Presidential Election Cycle Theory** was developed by Yale Hirsch, founder of the *Stock Trader's Almanac* , first published in 1967. Hirsch's research proposed that U.S. stock market returns follow a broadly consistent pattern across each four-year presidential term. Returns tend to be weakest early in a term and strengthen as the next election approaches.


The theory's reasoning is primarily political: new administrations typically focus on policy implementation in their first years, creating uncertainty. As the next election nears, incumbent presidents tend to prioritize economic stimulus, which Hirsch argued supports stronger market performance.


### 1.2 Average Returns by Year of the Presidential Cycle


According to data compiled in Hirsch's *Stock Trader's Almanac* , the Dow Jones Industrial Average has produced the following average annual returns by cycle year since 1896:

Pre-election years have historically stood out as the strongest across both datasets. Midterm years have been the most consistently muted. It is important to note that these samples are small — roughly 18 to 25 observations — and return ranges within each bucket are wide. These figures are descriptive, not predictive.


*Past performance does not guarantee future results.*


### 1.3 Does the Theory Hold Up in Practice?


The theory has not produced consistent results in recent administrations. The S&P 500 posted a 19% gain in 2017 (Year 1 of Trump's first term) and a 30% gain in 2013 (Year 1 of Obama's second term) — both well above the historical post-election average.


Many market researchers argue the patterns reflect statistical coincidence rather than presidential influence. Corporate earnings, global economic data, and Federal Reserve monetary policy tend to be larger, more consistent drivers of stock prices.


*SoFi —*[https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/presidential-election-cycle-theory/](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/presidential-election-cycle-theory/)

## Part 2. Midterm Elections and Stock Market Volatility: What History Shows


### 2.1 Why Midterm Election Years Tend to Be Volatile


Midterm election years have a well-documented association with weaker stock returns and elevated market volatility. Capital Group's analysis of more than 90 years of S&P 500 data identified elevated volatility as a persistent characteristic of midterm years.


The primary driver is not which party wins — it is the uncertainty leading up to Election Day. Policy questions around regulation, spending priorities, and economic direction create a more difficult environment for investors to assess.


*Capital Group —*[https://www.capitalgroup.com/advisor/insights/articles/midterm-elections-markets-5-charts.html](https://www.capitalgroup.com/advisor/insights/articles/midterm-elections-markets-5-charts.html)


### 2.2 The Post-Midterm Rebound Pattern


Despite muted returns during midterm years, markets have historically bounced back strongly in the 12 months that follow. According to Fidelity's research, the S&P 500 posted price gains in approximately 95% of all 12-month periods following midterm elections since 1938.


On average, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 5% during midterm years, then jumped to approximately 14% in the following 12 months. This pattern has held regardless of which party gained or lost congressional seats.


*Fidelity —*[https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/the-surprising-truth-about-midterms-and-stocks](https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/the-surprising-truth-about-midterms-and-stocks)


### 2.3 The 2026 Midterm Environment


The 2026 midterm elections arrive amid an unusually elevated level of investor uncertainty. The Economic Policy Uncertainty Index — produced by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis — surged to more than eight times its long-term average earlier in 2026. Questions around trade tariffs, oil prices, inflation, and Federal Reserve policy have all contributed.


Notably, Fidelity's analysis observes that periods of peak uncertainty have historically been poor timing signals for investors — extreme pessimism has often faded as market conditions clarified.

## Part 3. What Actually Drives Stock Markets in Election Years


### 3.1 Fundamentals Matter More Than Politics


Fidelity's research is direct on this point: corporate earnings, business investment, and broader economic conditions have historically been more important drivers of long-term stock returns than election outcomes. The annual return of the S&P 500 has been broadly similar in presidential election years and non-election years going back to 1927.


Citizens Bank's analysis of the previous 10 presidential election years found that the S&P 500 trended upward in the months leading up to most elections — with the notable exceptions of 2000 (dotcom bust) and 2008 (financial crisis), which were driven by macro factors unrelated to election outcomes.


*Citizens Bank —*[https://www.citizensbank.com/learning/how-election-years-impact-the-stock-market.aspx](https://www.citizensbank.com/learning/how-election-years-impact-the-stock-market.aspx)


### 3.2 Policy Uncertainty as a Volatility Driver


As the old market adage goes, markets dislike uncertainty. Election campaigns generate a continuous flow of competing policy proposals, forecasts, and predictions. This creates a broader range of potential outcomes for investors to weigh, which elevates volatility.


Once votes are counted, however, much of that uncertainty begins to fade — even if the policy environment never becomes fully clear. "Things rarely get to 'clear.' They just get to 'less unclear,' and that is usually enough for investors," said Denise Chisholm, Director of Quantitative Market Strategy at Fidelity.


### 3.3 Earnings and Capital Expenditure in 2026


As of mid-2026, corporate earnings remain a constructive backdrop. S&P 500 earnings growth for the second quarter of 2026 increased to approximately 47% year-over-year. Business spending, particularly capital expenditures related to AI infrastructure, has also remained resilient. These factors may carry greater weight for investors than the midterm election outcome itself.

## Part 5. Party Control, Sector Rotation, and Congressional Elections


### 5.1 Does Party Control of Congress Matter for Returns?


A 75-year review of S&P 500 performance by U.S. Bank investment strategists found no statistically significant relationship between which party controlled the White House and overall stock market returns. Unified party control did not produce reliably better results than divided government across the full period analyzed.


One pattern that did achieve statistical significance: periods of Democratic White House control combined with Republican congressional control were associated with positive three-month S&P 500 returns above the long-term average.


*ModWM —*[https://www.modwm.com/the-4-year-presidential-election-cycle-and-the-stock-market/](https://www.modwm.com/the-4-year-presidential-election-cycle-and-the-stock-market/)


### 5.2 Divided Government and Market Stability


From a market perspective, divided government can reduce the probability of sweeping policy changes, making the policy environment more predictable for businesses and investors. "Markets love gridlock," said Anu Gaggar of Fidelity. Research from Capital Group similarly found that control of Congress has had little impact on long-term investment returns.


This does not mean divided government always produces strong returns — only that the relationship between congressional control and market performance has been weaker than popular narratives suggest.


### 5.3 Sector-Level Impacts of Election Outcomes


While broad market returns have remained relatively stable across different political configurations, specific sectors can respond more sharply to election results. Defense and industrial sectors showed stronger performance following the 2016 election, reflecting expectations for policy support. Health care sectors have historically fared differently under different administrations.


These sector-level shifts represent real but relatively contained impacts. The S&P 500's annual return has been 13.8% from 2009–2017, 14% from 2017–2021, and approximately 11% since 2021 — demonstrating similar ranges across different administrations.


### 5.4 Midterm Seat Changes and Policy Expectations


Historically, the president's party tends to lose congressional seats in midterm elections. Markets are generally aware of this tendency and begin pricing in the likelihood of increased legislative gridlock well ahead of Election Day. By the time results arrive, much of the uncertainty has already been partially absorbed.


Investors watching sector dynamics during the 2026 midterm cycle may consider monitoring earnings guidance from companies in policy-sensitive industries, rather than relying solely on polling data.

## The Bottom Line


The **election year market impact** is real but often secondary to the economic fundamentals that have historically driven returns. Midterm years tend to bring elevated volatility and muted performance, followed by historically stronger rebounds.
